summary: Updates the iCalendar and vCard formats, RFC 5545 and RFC 6350, so that parameter values can include certain characters the earlier specifications forbade. It does this through an escaping mechanism for those characters.

eli5.summary: A rule said certain letters could never go inside a note field. This adds a way to write them anyway.

subtitle: A small caret-based escape scheme lets iCalendar and vCard parameter values carry double quotes and line breaks.

tldr.problem: iCalendar and vCard syntax forbids double-quote and control characters in parameter values, but extensions increasingly need at least double quotes and line feeds there.
tldr.mechanism: The ^ character becomes an escape character in parameter values: ^n stands for a line break, ^^ for a caret and ^' for a double quote.
tldr.outcome: Parameter values can now carry those characters while staying compatible with existing parsers. The RFC updates RFC 5545, RFC 6321, RFC 6350 and RFC 6351.

today: RFC 6868 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2013 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It updates RFC 5545, RFC 6321, RFC 6350 and RFC 6351.

sections.title: The Problem with Parameter Values
sections.content:
iCalendar (RFC 5545) describes calendar data and vCard (RFC 6350) describes contact data. Both use a similar text format in which a property has parameters and a value.

The syntax of both formats prevents a double-quote character or control characters in a parameter value, although property values may contain them. As extensions multiply, there is a need to allow at least double quotes and line feeds. The \ escaping used for property text is not defined for parameters and cannot easily be used in a backwards-compatible way, so this RFC defines a new mechanism.
sections.eli5: A form box refused quotation marks and new lines. People kept needing them, so a new trick was made to sneak them in.

sections.title: The Caret Escape Scheme
sections.content:
The ^ character (U+005E, Circumflex Accent) is defined as an escape character in parameter values that use the param-value syntax element. It works whether or not the value is surrounded by double quotes.

When generating values, a formatted text line break becomes ^n, a ^ becomes ^^, and a double quote becomes ^'. When parsing, the reverse applies: ^n becomes a line break suited to the system, ^^ becomes ^, and ^' becomes a double quote.

If a ^ is followed by any other character, parsers MUST leave both the caret and the following character in place. When converting to XML forms such as xCal (RFC 6321) and xCard (RFC 6351), implementations MUST make sure escape sequences are generated correctly in the text format and decoded when the values appear in the XML form.
sections.eli5: Write ^n when you want a new line, ^' when you want a quotation mark, and ^^ when you really want a caret. Anything else is left alone.

sections.title: iCalendar and vCard Examples
sections.content:
In iCalendar, an ATTENDEE property has a CN parameter whose value contains two double quotes. The value is not quoted, because nothing in it triggers quoting. The unescaped value is George Herman "Babe" Ruth.

In vCard, a GEO property has an X-ADDRESS parameter containing several line feeds. The value is quoted because it contains a comma, and each line break is written ^n.
sections.eli5: The name with quotes around Babe is typed with ^' marks, and an address with several lines is typed on one line with ^n between the parts.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states that there are no additional security issues beyond those of iCalendar (RFC 5545) and vCard (RFC 6350). The escape scheme only changes how certain characters are written in parameter values.
sections.eli5: The new spelling trick does not open any new doors for trouble beyond the ones that already existed.

sections.title: Why a Caret and Not a Backslash
sections.content:
The obvious choice was the \ escaping used for property values, but that escapes a double quote as a backslash followed by a double quote. Existing parsers know nothing about escapes in parameters, so they would stop at that second double quote and could legitimately report a syntax error. For backwards compatibility a double quote cannot be escaped by a sequence containing a double quote, hence the single quote in ^'.

A modified backslash scheme for parameters was rejected because incorrect, non-interoperable use of \ in parameter values has been observed, and because it could suggest that property and parameter escaping share code. The ^ was chosen as an ASCII symbol that is least likely to be found in existing data.
sections.eli5: The old trick would confuse old programs, like a door code that sets off the old alarm. So a different, quieter symbol was picked.
